w: Hole-in-the-wall named after the Miles Davis track, crate-dug vinyl stacked beside JBL speakers and mismatched Simpsons-era furniture. Northern Thai boat noodles and khao soi come from the owner's Lampang upbringing, congee sets and house sausage too. Records spin while you eat, breakfast till the needle drops.
s: Thai boat noodles under a wall of vinyl
why: Broadsheet and local food press called it one of Brisbane's buzziest 2025 openings

w: Thirty square metres inside a shipping container, wedged beside the Bunnings car park entrance on Breakfast Creek Road. Coffee Supreme through a La Marzocco, matcha, batch brew and cheesy toasties from a hatch window. Locals swear it makes the best coffee ever attached to a hardware store.
s: Coffee cart in a shipping container by Bunnings
why: Went viral online as 'the Bunnings car park cafe', covered by Broadsheet and Newstead News in 2025

w: Half sandwich shop, half bingsu bar, from Sophie Xu and Ted Chen, who noticed Korean shaved ice barely existed outside Sunnybank. Each flavour gets its own milk base rather than one shared block: taro, black sesame, earl grey and Thai tea, plus a coconut-mango vegan version, alongside Japanese-style sandos.
s: Korean shaved ice with a base for every flavour
why: Concrete Playground and local press flagged it as 2025's West End sleeper hit

w: Pint-sized Albion bakery from Falco and Proud Mary alumni, open Friday to Sunday mornings only and reliably sold out by lunchtime. Flaky lamination, cardamom buns and small-batch precision have made it a contender for Brisbane's best croissant within months of opening, queues forming before the roller door goes up.
s: Weekend-only bakery selling out its croissants by noon
why: Named a 2025 highlight by The Weekend Edition and Broadsheet Brisbane

w: Merivale's first Melbourne venue, opened late 2025 in the old Lily Blacks space on Meyers Place. Vinyl pulled from local record stores spins through DJ sets, agave-forward cocktails poured in low light, retro-futurist decor from Zara and Michael Madrusan, the pair behind The Everleigh a few doors down.
s: Sydney's Merivale group lands in a vinyl-only laneway bar
why: Wallpaper and Gourmet Traveller covered its late-2025 opening as a major Melbourne bar debut

w: Japanese-inspired listening bar on Enmore Road, built around a serious hi-fi and shelves of records, cocktails and late bites served while a curated soundtrack actually gets listened to. Doors stay open past midnight weekends, with karaoke nights added soon after launch.
s: A listening bar where the hi-fi is the main act
why: Broadsheet and Time Out named it one of Enmore's standout 2025 openings

w: Tucked into Lithgow Street, this Vietnamese-Melbourne cafe pours ca phe trung, the traditional whipped egg coffee, alongside a hojicha matcha and a salted-cream iced coffee that reliably fills social feeds. Garlic cheese bread and Basque cheesecake round out a small, photogenic menu.
s: Vietnamese egg coffee in a Melbourne side-street cafe
why: Viral on TikTok and Lemon8 through 2025 for its egg coffee and matcha cloud drinks

w: Long-running Japanese matcha brand's first Australian shop, opened inside a former cafe corner on King William Street. Ceremonial-grade whisked matcha, matcha soft-serve and matcha sweets are made to order at a small counter, a slow ritual dropped into a fast CBD strip since its January opening.
s: A Japanese matcha house's first Australian outpost
why: Broadsheet and Glam Adelaide covered its debut as Adelaide's biggest matcha opening yet

w: Award-winning bathing brand's newest outpost, a step off Chapel Street with mineral soaking pools, a dry cedarwood sauna, steam room and cold plunge across 700 square metres. Opened mid-2025 in a rapid national rollout, it turned mineral bathing into a weekday tram-line ritual.
s: Mineral pools and cold plunge a tram ride off Chapel Street
why: Time Out and Concrete Playground covered its July 2025 opening as part of Soak's expansion

w: Reached through a rear laneway between James and Francis Streets, this split-level rooftop sits among Northbridge's heritage roofs with a retractable roof and communal wooden tables. Unpolished and brick-walled, it looks over the cultural precinct and skyline, the bar every Perth visitor gets pointed toward.
s: Hidden rooftop reached through a Northbridge laneway
why: Consistently topped 2025 hidden-gem and rooftop-bar roundups for Perth

w: Australia's first branch of the international illusion-museum franchise, opened December 2025 on George Street with over 80 rooms playing tricks on depth, gravity and scale: a vortex tunnel, an upside-down room, holograms and optical setups built for photos that do not look real.
s: Eighty rooms of optical trickery on George Street
why: Time Out and Broadsheet covered its December 2025 opening as Australia's first Museum of Illusions

w: Interactive mini golf, an arcade and a rooftop bar stacked into one Hindley Street venue, billed on opening as Australia's first digitally-projected mini golf using real clubs and real balls against a projected course. Open nightly from 6pm with live DJs, it turned a late-bar strip into a game room.
s: Real clubs, digital-projection mini golf on Hindley Street
why: Glam Adelaide covered its October 2025 opening as one of the CBD's buzziest new venues

w: Husband-and-wife opening from Danny Lee and Dianne Cho on New North Road, a small euro-leaning menu of grilled leeks with chorizo and soft-boiled egg alongside considered filter coffee and matcha. Warm timber and an unhurried pace made it one of Eden Terrace's most talked-about new rooms.
s: Considered coffee and euro brunch in Eden Terrace
why: The Denizen and Eat It Auckland flagged it among Auckland's best late-2025 openings

w: Ground-floor coffee spot on High Street, sneaked between shopfronts opposite the big Pride mural stairs in a 1930s building, plant-filled and lit in the pink neon that gives it its name. Run by Rosie and Hayley with a resident dog behind the counter, it spread almost entirely through short-form video.
s: Plant-filled coffee nook lit entirely in pink neon
why: Repeatedly filmed and reshared on TikTok through 2025 as Auckland CBD's hidden coffee spot

w: Sleek fit-out inside the restored NZR Co building on Hereford Street, running Ozone Coffee through a Modbar setup with cold foam drinks and simple cabinet food. Opened in a building once known locally as a graffiti eyesore, it has become a symbol of the block's post-earthquake comeback.
s: Modbar coffee inside a restored heritage building
why: Neat Places and NZ Herald flagged it among Christchurch's best 2025 openings

w: Husband-and-wife brewery built by hand inside a former glass manufacturing building on the corner of Orbell and Disraeli Streets, self-fitted with recycled materials and timber to keep the industrial bones exposed. Opened April 2025 as a working brew bar and taproom in Sydenham's industrial grid.
s: Taproom self-built inside an old glass factory
why: Neat Places named it among Christchurch's standout 2025 openings

w: Michael Chan's follow-up to his long-running KC Cafe, opened on Cuba Street with Peking duck, hand-pulled baos, tom yum and Sichuan chicken reworked for a room built for lingering rather than quick lunches. Chan first sketched it during the 2020 lockdown; it became Wellington's most talked-about 2025 opening.
s: KC Cafe's owner brings Peking duck to Cuba Street
why: The Spinoff profiled it as Wellington's most anticipated 2025 restaurant follow-up

w: Once-quiet Bayside car parks and laneways around Station Street and Gallery Lane now carry over 70 large-scale murals from an annual international street art festival, turning a commuter town an hour from the CBD into an open-air gallery. Self-guided trails start at Frankston Library.
s: Seventy-plus murals turned a car park into a gallery
why: Frankston was recently ranked among the world's best street art cities on the back of this festival

w: Boronia Park's first-ever night market, launched April 2026 on the last Friday of each month, with more than thirty stalls of street food and handmade goods, roving performers and local musicians filling a suburban park not previously known for nightlife or weekday crowds.
s: A suburban park's first-ever monthly night market
why: Time Out and City of Parramatta covered its launch as a new fixture for Sydney's northwest

w: Level 4 of the Hilton Sydney reopens each warmer season as a gin-branded secret garden, lush with greenery over a rooftop terrace facing the Queen Victoria Building. A hidden door marks the entrance; inside, garden cocktails, live music and high tea keep the transformation trending on video.
s: A hidden door opens onto a rooftop gin garden
why: A recurring TikTok favourite, repeatedly filmed as Sydney's viral secret garden bar
